chunks: Muhammad ibn Ahmad from Ya'qub ibn Yazid from Marwak ibn Ubayd from some of our companions from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

I asked him: 'A man passes by a crop field and takes a single ear of grain from it.' He said: 'No.' I asked: 'What is the ear of grain?' He said: 'If everyone who passes by it were to take a single ear, nothing would remain.'
Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar said: I wrote to him:

A man who precedes caravans on his own authority (not by command of the ruler) in a place of fear, and they make a specific agreement with him that he should take from them when they reach safety. Is it permissible for him to take from them or not? So he (peace be upon him) wrote: 'If he hires himself out for a known amount, he takes his right, if God wills.'

key_terms.يُشَارِطُونَهُ: they make an agreement with him

ai.seo_question: Is it permissible for a private individual to take payment for guarding caravans without being appointed by the ruler?
ai.summary: In the first narration, Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies that taking a single ear of grain is permissible by citing the principle of 'non-depletion' (la darar), warning that if everyone took one, the crop would vanish, thus establishing a limit based on customary practice. The second narration addresses the fiqh of 'ijarah' (contract of employment), ruling that a private individual guarding caravans in dangerous areas without official appointment is entitled to the agreed-upon compensation, highlighting the validity of private contracts in Shia jurisprudence. These rulings underscore the flexibility of commercial transactions in Shia law, balancing individual rights with communal benefit.
